title: Can AI Be More Persuasive Than a Human Lawyer? — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The supplied source evidence is limited to host introductions and a personal discussion of open-water swimming. It contains no substantive claims about legal AI, task-level capability, verification, selective deployment or operating-model redesign, so its position relative to the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: AI simulation: Practice substitutes remain unvalidated
st.an: The source accepts AI simulation as a prospective supplement for advocacy practice and materially extends the proposition to solos, small firms and other lawyers lacking institutional rehearsal support. It also proposes real-time feedback and distinguishes written from oral advocacy, while offering no measured evidence that these tools improve outcomes.
qs: For lawyers in small firms, solos, or those assigned to high-stakes cases like termination of parental rights without institutional support — they often didn’t have anyone to moot with.
But with this technology, they could build a tool, practice with it, and get real-time feedback on each persuasive move they try.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts and materially extends the cluster’s proposed reconstruction of training by specifying AI-enabled negotiation simulations, persuasion curricula, critical comparison of AI and human arguments, and real-time advocacy feedback. Its arithmetic-error anecdote also reinforces the need for human verification. It does not, however, establish the broader claim that automation is eroding apprenticeship or expertise reproduction; its training benefits remain proposals rather than measured outcomes.
qs: One day we’ll look back and think it’s crazy how we used to teach negotiation: “Here are some techniques that worked for me in practice.” When instead, we could be simulating thousands of negotiation styles, instantly tailoring based on context, stakes, or personality type.
It gave me a whole analysis, and I thought, “Wow, I’m in a great spot!” But when I checked the math, there was a huge miscalculation.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts AI as an augmentative collaborator rather than a substitute for lawyers and materially extends the cluster by identifying persuasion, counterargument development, advocacy rehearsal and curriculum design as concrete workflows. Its claims are largely proposals and predictions, however, not evidence of improved legal outcomes, and it gives less attention to verification than the cluster does.
qs: It just feels like an incredibly powerful collaborator for developing persuasive strategies — and that’s core to lawyering.
Honestly, law schools should be developing curriculum modules right now around using this tech for persuasion.

st.t: AI competition: Distribution and habits rival capability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of a capability shift toward agentic systems that autonomously select and combine tools. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution toward AGI claims, noting definitional disagreement. It does not materially address the separate distribution-and-user-habits thesis.
qs: I gave it one task that required both web research and code — and it showed me the code it was running as it worked.
That said, nobody really agrees on what AGI is.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty by presenting AI as an augmentative thinking and learning partner and urging professionals to reconsider where they add value. Its claims rest mainly on personal experience and hypotheses, with an anecdotal example of AI overemphasis, so it aligns with the cluster’s distinction between useful experimentation and demonstrated reliability.
qs: We’ve all been so focused on mastering these skills ourselves, but the models are now either matching us or supporting us so powerfully that we need to redefine where our value lies in professional settings.
For me, I think what I’m realizing now is that it would’ve been a multiplier — it would’ve helped me understand things much more deeply.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the engagement-first proposition by arguing that professionals should actively redefine their value as AI capabilities advance. It reinforces the cluster’s anticipated shift toward distinctively human professional contributions, but does not materially develop implementation, governance or public-interest participation.
qs: We’ve all been so focused on mastering these skills ourselves, but the models are now either matching us or supporting us so powerfully that we need to redefine where our value lies in professional settings.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s framing of AI as lawyer augmentation applied to concrete workflows rather than wholesale replacement. It identifies persuasion-specific uses, audience and confidentiality considerations, and a training implication, while offering little direct analysis of the organisational incentives, leadership or infrastructure needed for adoption.
qs: If you’re using an enterprise platform, you can already start feeding your matter into it and asking for help with persuasion — just tell it who you’re trying to persuade.
Honestly, law schools should be developing curriculum modules right now around using this tech for persuasion.

kp.k: Reported Reddit study found substantially higher AI persuasion rates
kp.d: Leonard describes University of Zurich researchers deploying AI-generated counterarguments on Change My View, engaging with over a thousand unique posts. Success meant the original poster awarded a triangle icon indicating a changed view. She reports personalized responses succeeding at 18%, generic responses at 17%, and community-aligned responses around 9%, against a human baseline of about 3%. Personalization inferred characteristics from prior public posts; community alignment mirrored subreddit style and norms. These are reported online-discussion findings, while their implications for legal advocacy are the speakers’ extrapolations.
qs: These bots engaged with over a thousand unique posts.

Personalized AI responses had an 18% success rate in changing someone’s mind. Compare that to the human baseline which was about 3% successful at persuading people to change their view. Even the generic AI response came in at 17%. The community-aligned AI was less effective but still far better than humans — around 9%.

kp.k: Undisclosed chatbot deployment raised research ethics concerns
kp.d: Leonard notes that users were not told bots were participating. She reports the researchers’ justification that awareness of observation changes behavior in controlled studies, motivating research in a real-world setting; this is their reported rationale, not an independently established resolution of the ethical issue.
qs: they had AI chatbots generate some of the counterarguments without telling users that bots were involved.

So there’s controversy on the research ethics side, but the authors argued that research is already “contaminated” in some sense — people know they’re being observed in controlled studies, which changes their behavior.

kp.k: AI could collaborate on persuasive legal strategy
kp.d: McCormack recommends using AI to support persuasion in transactions, litigation, arbitration, and client counseling. Leonard proposes identifying blind spots, anticipating opposing arguments, and improving framing. McCormack suggests specifying the intended audience, using an enterprise platform for matter-based work, or abstracting private details when using a personal Plus subscription. The proposed role is lawyer augmentation rather than direct substitution.
qs: Persuasion is such a fundamental legal skill — whether you’re negotiating a deal, in a transactional setting, in litigation or arbitration, trying to convince a judge or a jury, or even persuading your own client about a course of action.
You can describe the setting, the legal context, the challenge, and ask for different ways to frame an argument or anticipate counterarguments.

kp.k: Leonard predicts competitive disadvantages from foregoing AI
kp.d: Leonard reframes adoption ethics around the risks of not using AI, arguing that lawyers should assume opposing counsel, co-counsel, judges, and corporate clients already use it. She predicts serious disadvantages for unaided advocacy; this is a forceful practitioner forecast rather than a measured legal-market outcome.
qs: But I try to help lawyers think differently: what are the risks of not using this technology?
So if you show up without an AI-enhanced strategy for persuasion, you’re at a serious disadvantage.

kp.k: Client AI critiques may reshape lawyer-client exchanges
kp.d: Leonard attributes to her colleague Mariel the prediction that lawyers will increasingly need to respond to AI critiques of their work product, and proposes preparing persuasive responses to client objections. McCormack emphasizes that the client might be right and recommends asking AI to evaluate both positions and conduct reciprocal persuasion, while avoiding sycophantic feedback.
qs: my brilliant colleague Mariel has pointed out that lawyers will increasingly have to respond to AI critiques of their work product.
Maybe not. But either way, you could input both arguments: “Here’s what I’m thinking. Here’s what the client is thinking. Evaluate both. If I’m wrong, persuade me.”

kp.k: Legal education should incorporate AI persuasion exercises
kp.d: McCormack calls for immediate curriculum development around AI-assisted persuasion. Leonard envisages simulations of thousands of negotiation styles tailored to context, stakes, or personality, and exercises analyzing why an AI argument is more persuasive than a human baseline. She distinguishes written advocacy, which resembles the Reddit setting, from oral advocacy involving live interaction and nonverbal communication, raising questions about training and assessment.
qs: Honestly, law schools should be developing curriculum modules right now around using this tech for persuasion.
I could see an exercise where students are asked to explain why an AI-generated argument is more persuasive than a human baseline, and unpack what that means in practice.
I’m also curious about the difference between brief writing — which feels closer to the Reddit example, where there's no live interaction or nonverbal communication — versus oral advocacy.

kp.k: AI practice partners could support under-resourced advocates
kp.d: Drawing on her ten years on the bench and the varying quality of state supreme court advocacy, McCormack suggests AI could provide rehearsal and real-time feedback for solos, small-firm lawyers, and advocates handling high-stakes matters without institutional support. Leonard speculates about combining persuasive tools with avatar or presentation-feedback systems to improve nonverbal delivery.
qs: For lawyers in small firms, solos, or those assigned to high-stakes cases like termination of parental rights without institutional support — they often didn’t have anyone to moot with.
But with this technology, they could build a tool, practice with it, and get real-time feedback on each persuasive move they try.

kp.k: Lawyer value may shift toward contextualization and counseling
kp.d: McCormack conditionally predicts a professional role shift if AI becomes better at writing arguments, explaining them, and identifying logical breakdowns. She expressly qualifies that the technology cannot yet do everything described, while arguing that its matching or supporting existing skills already prompts reconsideration of professional value.
qs: Because if the technology can make the arguments better than humans can — and I’m not saying it can do all that yet, but it’s getting close — then maybe our role shifts.

If it can write the arguments better, if it can explain them more clearly, if it can tell you when your logic breaks down, then maybe the lawyer’s job becomes translating, contextualizing, and counseling people through what it means and what to do next.

kp.k: Reasoning models increasingly select tools and execute multistep work
kp.d: McCormack reports releases of OpenAI o3 and o4-mini and Google Gemini 2.5, highlighting o3’s visual-input capabilities and autonomous selection among web research, image generation, and coding. Her examples include correcting a company-name typo and combining research with code. Both speakers describe reduced manual model and tool selection as a practical improvement; benchmark praise is unspecific, and these examples are personal experience.
qs: The feature I love most is that with O3, you can ask it a question, and it decides which of the tools in its suite it needs to use to get you the best answer.
I gave it one task that required both web research and code — and it showed me the code it was running as it worked.
Before, you had to choose a tool manually — dropdowns, model versions, all that.

kp.k: Capability gains coexist with errors requiring human checking
kp.d: Leonard says earlier reasoning models showed promise with legal nuance and that RAG helped reduce hallucinations, but reports hearing that newer reasoning models may hallucinate more. Her concrete example is a major retirement-planning arithmetic error she caught and had o3 correct, not a measured hallucination rate. McCormack also reports hearing concerns online without having noticed them herself. The discussion presents uneven progress rather than established reliability improvements across tasks.
qs: And retrieval-augmented generation — RAG — has helped reduce hallucinations.
That said, I’ve heard the newest reasoning models might actually hallucinate more.
But when I checked the math, there was a huge miscalculation. I pointed it out, and to its credit, it redid everything.

kp.k: Memory and sycophancy complicate independent AI feedback
kp.d: The speakers describe memory as useful for personalized reflection but potentially distracting. Leonard attributes to Ethan Mollick the concern that unrelated history or attempts to please a user can contaminate new answers, and says she disabled memory; McCormack suggests instructing the system to exclude earlier conversations. Separately, McCormack reports that OpenAI rolled back tuning after excessive agreement in the model she calls GPT-4.0. These concerns matter to their proposed uses for critique and persuasion practice.
qs: But Ethan Mollick made an interesting point — that when memory is toggled on, it can contaminate a new response by pulling in unrelated past information or it might try to please you based on your past preferences, even if it’s not relevant to the current query.
I actually toggled “memory” off completely.
I thought that was fascinating — that it got so sycophantic they actually rolled back the tuning on the model.

kp.k: Conversational AI may deepen learning and legal reasoning
kp.d: Leonard reports learning and processing more effectively through voice interaction and hypothesizes that such dialogue would have deepened her understanding as a junior litigator. McCormack similarly values reciprocal discussion and suspects it improves legal writing. These are personal learning observations and educational hypotheses, not comparative evidence about learner outcomes.
qs: I process more, and I’m more productive. Honestly, I’m more excited about learning when I do it that way.
Even though writing is obviously an important craft for lawyers, I bet the ability to reason through something actually makes writing better. That’s my strong suspicion.

kp.k: AI streamlines practical research, synthesis, and administrative drafting
kp.d: McCormack describes using ChatGPT to compare recording arrangements for an in-person June workshop with probably 150+ people, assess whether existing tools sufficed, recommend a setup, and draft AV instructions. She characterizes this as more efficient than searching and independently synthesizing results. The example demonstrates her changed administrative workflow rather than measured legal-task productivity.
qs: It walked me through all the pros and cons, and I finally had it make a recommendation.
If I had gone to Google to figure this out, maybe I would’ve found a Consumer Reports review eventually, but it would’ve taken forever and I’d still have to synthesize and write it myself.

kp.k: AI-mediated discovery may change professional content marketing
kp.d: Leonard recalls ChatGPT sourcing legal preparation notes from Skadden and Davis Wright Tremaine blogs and wonders how marketers secure AI visibility. McCormack speculates that AI optimization overlaps with SEO but requires new techniques. The transcript offers anecdotal sourcing observations and marketing conjecture, not evidence of market-wide displacement of search.
qs: when I asked ChatGPT for prep notes, it pulled sources from blogs by firms like Skadden and Davis Wright Tremaine.
I’m sure AI Optimization is similar to SEO, maybe with some overlap in strategy — but I think it requires new techniques too.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack and Leonard argue that AI can already augment lawyers’ persuasive strategy by identifying blind spots, anticipating counterarguments and proposing alternative framing.
pts.d: McCormack proposes using AI as a collaborator in transactional negotiations, litigation, arbitration, advocacy before judges and juries, and counseling clients. Leonard describes adding AI to the deliberation that would otherwise occur between colleagues. Their proposed use is augmentation, not autonomous representation. McCormack conditions matter-specific use on an enterprise platform or abstraction of private information when using a personal subscription.

pts.k: Leonard predicts a serious competitive disadvantage for lawyers who do not use AI-enhanced persuasion.
pts.d: Leonard presents non-use as an increasing professional risk and says lawyers should assume opposing counsel, co-counsel, judges and corporate clients already use AI. This is her strategic assertion, not a reported measurement of adoption or litigation outcomes. She also asserts that opponents using presentation-coaching tools to refine their presence will be more persuasive.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack propose using AI to handle client challenges to lawyers’ advice and to test whether the lawyer’s own position is sound.
pts.d: Leonard develops a practical use case in which a lawyer prepares a response to a client’s AI-generated objection. The underlying prediction that lawyers will increasingly face AI critiques is explicitly credited in the transcript to Leonard’s colleague Mariel; Leonard’s own contribution is the tooling-gap concern and proposed response. McCormack adds that the client might be right and suggests having AI evaluate both positions and conduct a back-and-forth persuasion exercise. She qualifies this use by requiring a non-sycophantic model.

pts.k: The speakers foresee AI changing legal education through tailored negotiation simulations, argument analysis and conversational learning.
pts.d: McCormack calls for persuasion curriculum modules immediately. Leonard envisages simulations of thousands of negotiation styles tailored to context, stakes and personality, and exercises analyzing why an AI-generated argument is more persuasive than a human baseline. Separately, Leonard reports that voice interaction improves her own processing, productivity and enthusiasm for learning; McCormack suspects conversational reasoning can improve lawyers’ writing. These educational effects are proposed or personally inferred, rather than demonstrated by an educational study.

pts.k: McCormack argues that AI could provide advocacy practice and real-time feedback to lawyers who lack institutional support.
pts.d: She identifies solo and small-firm lawyers, inexperienced advocates and lawyers assigned high-stakes matters such as termination of parental rights. Her claim concerns making moot practice and coaching available where colleagues or institutional resources are absent. Leonard additionally speculates about combining persuasion tools with avatars or tools that assess nonverbal behavior. Neither reports a measured improvement in legal outcomes from such a system.

pts.k: McCormack conditionally predicts that lawyers’ value may shift toward translation, contextualization and counseling as AI becomes better at constructing and explaining arguments.
pts.d: McCormack does not claim that AI can already perform every advocacy function better than lawyers. Her role-shift prediction depends on AI becoming capable of writing better arguments, explaining them clearly and identifying broken logic. She nevertheless says models are already matching lawyers or supporting them strongly enough to prompt reconsideration of professional value. She does not attach a date or quantify employment effects.

pts.k: McCormack describes reasoning models as reducing the need for users to select tools manually and reports substantial workflow efficiencies from AI assistance.
pts.d: McCormack says o3 can select among web research, coding and image tools, handle mistakes in a query, and reason with visual inputs. Her examples concern company research and planning an in-person workshop, not completed legal matters. In the workshop example, AI helped compare recording arrangements and draft instructions for the AV team. The relevance to legal work is a claimed improvement in general professional workflows rather than a measured law-firm productivity effect.

pts.k: Leonard qualifies capability improvements with concerns about reliability, irrelevant personalization and the difficulty of persuading lawyers to adopt error-prone models.
pts.d: Leonard says earlier reasoning models showed promise in capturing legal nuance and that retrieval-augmented generation helped reduce hallucinations, while reporting that she has heard newer reasoning models may hallucinate more. Her direct error example is a substantial retirement-planning miscalculation she caught and had corrected; it is not a measured hallucination rate or a legal citation fabrication. She also reports turning memory off because irrelevant personal details intruded into answers. McCormack proposes prompting the model not to consider previous conversations, saying this can help produce a cleaner response.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal empirical basis is a reported University of Zurich Reddit persuasion study, not a comparison between AI and practicing lawyers.
pts.d: Leonard recounts researchers deploying undisclosed AI-generated replies to more than a thousand unique Change My View posts. Success meant receiving the original poster’s triangle icon indicating a changed view. She reports approximately 18% success for personalized replies, 17% for generic replies, 9% for community-aligned replies and 3% for the human baseline. Personalization used inferred characteristics from publicly available posting histories; community alignment mirrored subreddit style and norms. These are study findings as reported by Leonard and attributed to the researchers, not research conducted by the speakers. Both acknowledge controversy over undisclosed bot participation. The transcript provides no corresponding test of briefs, oral arguments, negotiations or legal outcomes.

pts.k: The legal applications and role predictions rest chiefly on professional experience, personal tool use and extrapolation from the persuasion study.
pts.d: McCormack draws on ten years of reading briefs and hearing oral arguments as a judge to identify uneven advocacy quality and lack of practice support. Leonard draws on her experience as a junior litigator and current voice-mode use. McCormack’s workflow claims rely on her own o3 and workshop-planning examples. The speakers offer no quantified legal productivity, learning, adoption or competitive-outcome evidence. McCormack refers to strong benchmark performance without naming tests or reporting scores. Predictions of competitive disadvantage and a shift in lawyers’ value are the speakers’ inferences.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The episode presents strategic assistance as available now in 2025, while treating educational transformation and role redefinition as undated future possibilities.
pts.d: McCormack says lawyers can already use enterprise systems or abstracted prompts for persuasion and urges curriculum development now. Leonard frames competitive risk as already increasing. Advocacy coaching and large-scale negotiation simulations are possibilities rather than completed deployments. McCormack’s role-shift prediction is explicitly conditional on superior argument generation and explanation. Leonard distinguishes written persuasion from live advocacy and leaves the implications for training and assessment open. Reliability, confidentiality, sycophancy and memory relevance qualify the proposed uses. No specific date is supplied for profession-wide transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects span advocates, transactional lawyers, clients, law students and especially lawyers without substantial institutional support.
pts.d: Litigators, arbitration counsel and transactional lawyers gain proposed strategy and rehearsal tools. Solos, small firms and lawyers handling high-stakes assigned matters could gain feedback otherwise unavailable to them. Clients, including corporate clients, may use AI to challenge advice and become audiences for AI-assisted counseling. Opposing counsel, co-counsel and judges enter Leonard’s assumption about an AI-equipped professional environment, rather than a documented adoption finding. Law schools and students face proposed changes to persuasion teaching and assessment. The public appears indirectly through consequential matters such as termination of parental rights; the episode does not quantify unmet legal need or claim a measured access-to-justice improvement.
